name: Latency and Round Trips
intent: See why distance and the number of back-and-forth exchanges decide how fast a request feels, and how to reduce both with caching, nearby servers and fewer handshakes.
scenario: A user in Sydney opens a site hosted in Virginia. The server answers in 20 ms, yet the page still takes most of a second to start. The delay is not computing, it is the number of times the signal has to cross the Pacific.
problem: Data travels no faster than the speed of light in fibre, about 200,000 km per second, so a round trip of 15,000 km each way takes at least 150 ms, and real routes are longer. Establishing a secure connection takes several round trips before the first byte of the page moves. You cannot make light faster, so the only fixes are to make fewer trips and shorten each one.

howItWorks.title: Latency is mostly distance
howItWorks.text: Round trip time (RTT) is the time for a message to go out and the reply to come back. Within a city it is a few milliseconds, across a continent tens, and between continents 100 to 300 ms. Bandwidth does not fix it: a bigger pipe does not shorten the distance.

howItWorks.title: Count the round trips before the first byte
howItWorks.text: A fresh HTTPS request needs a DNS lookup, a TCP handshake (1 round trip), a TLS handshake (1 round trip for TLS 1.3, 2 for TLS 1.2) and then the request itself (1 round trip). That can be four or five round trips, so at 150 ms each the user waits most of a second before seeing anything.

howItWorks.title: Remove round trips
howItWorks.text: Reuse connections (keep-alive and HTTP/2) so the handshakes happen once. Use TLS 1.3 and QUIC (HTTP/3) to cut handshakes, and session resumption (skipping part of the handshake for a returning visitor) for repeat visits. Cache DNS answers. Combine or avoid requests that depend on each other so they do not queue.

howItWorks.title: Shorten the trips
howItWorks.text: Serve users from a nearby location: a CDN (content delivery network) edge answers the handshakes from a few milliseconds away and reuses a warm connection to the origin. Replicate data or run services in several regions so users are close to a copy.

howItWorks.title: Remember sequential dependencies
howItWorks.text: Calls that wait for each other add up: a page that fetches a list, then each item, then each item's images has three round trips in a row. Fetch in parallel where possible, and prefer APIs that return what a screen needs in one call.

pros: Thinking in round trips explains most 'why is it slow when the server is fast?' puzzles
Fewer round trips improves every user, especially on mobile and far from your servers
CDNs, connection reuse and modern protocols give large gains with little code
Makes trade-offs such as multi-region deployments concrete
cons: Moving servers and data closer adds cost and consistency problems
Edge caching only helps for cacheable content
Faster handshakes depend on client and server support
Optimising for distant users can complicate architecture
whenToUse: Any user-facing service with users far from the origin
Diagnosing slow first loads, where the server time is small
Capacity and regional planning: where to place servers and caches
whenNotToUse: Optimising network trips when the real cost is a slow database query or heavy computation: measure first
Internal calls within one data centre, where a round trip is a fraction of a millisecond
pitfalls: Testing only on a fast local network, where latency never shows
Chaining dependent requests in a loop (the N+1 problem over the network)
Handshaking on every request because connections are not reused
Assuming a bigger bandwidth plan will speed up small requests

roles.label: Nearby edge
roles.description: A CDN or regional server a few milliseconds away.

quiz.question: A user in Sydney opens a page from a server in Virginia, with a round trip of about 200 ms. The server answers in 20 ms, yet the page takes about a second to start. The content is cacheable. Which change helps most?
options: Buy a faster internet plan for the origin, since more bandwidth moves the page sooner
Upgrade the origin to faster CPUs to cut the 20 ms processing time
Serve it through a CDN edge near Sydney, so handshakes end close to the user
Compress all images harder to reduce the amount of data sent
quiz.explanation: The delay is several round trips (DNS, TCP, TLS, request), counting each as 200 ms, and the CDN makes each of them a few milliseconds. Bandwidth, CPU and image size do not shorten the distance.

quiz.question: A mobile app fetches a list of 20 items and then calls the server once per item for its details, one after another. The network round trip is 100 ms and the server work per item is tiny. You want the fewest round trips. What is the best change?
options: Run the 20 detail calls in parallel, which cuts the total to about two trips
Add one endpoint that returns the list with its details in a single trip
Move the servers to faster hardware so each detail call finishes sooner
Cache the detail responses on the phone for the next time the list is opened
quiz.explanation: The cost is the number of trips, so a single call that returns what the screen needs wins, down to one round trip. Parallel calls still need a second trip, and faster hardware attacks the tiny server time.

quiz.question: A backend service calls a partner API in another region, 80 ms away, and opens a new HTTPS connection for every request using TLS 1.3. Each call takes about 240 ms. What is the best fix?
options: Reuse connections with keep-alive or a pool, so only the request round trip is paid
Move to a plan with more bandwidth so that the handshake data can transfer much faster
Switch to TLS 1.2 with a shorter certificate chain, which can be set up with fewer round trips
Compress the request bodies so fewer bytes travel over each connection
quiz.explanation: A new connection costs a TCP round trip and a TLS 1.3 round trip before the request round trip, which is 3 x 80 = 240 ms. A reused connection pays only the 80 ms. Bandwidth and compression shrink the bytes, not the trips. TLS 1.2 needs more round trips, not fewer.
